title: Family of man who died after Toronto police altercation sues for $5M
article: The family of a man who died after an altercation with Toronto police in his apartment last year is suing the police board and 10 unidentified officers, seeking $5 million.

In a statement of claim filed in Ontario's Superior Court last month, the family of Rodrigo Gonzalez alleges his death was a "direct result of the physical assault and battery perpetrated against him" by the police. Photographs taken by Gonzalez's family at the hospital show a head injury wrapped in bloody gauze, as well as a black eye, bruising on a limb and shoulder, and what the family suspects is a Taser mark near his groin.
The allegations in the statement of claim have not been proven in court.
Toronto Police spokesperson Mark Pugash said the Toronto Police Services Board was served with the lawsuit last month. "We will be putting out a statement of defence in due course," he said.

According to the statement of claim, Gonzalez, a 43-year-old father of two, who was 5 feet 4 inches tall and weighed 145 pounds, died in the intensive care unit at St. Joseph's Health Centre on Nov. 7.

The death "likely resulted from cardiac arrest second to profound hypoxemia," the claim says. Gonzalez's wife, Susana, had called 911 two days earlier because the couple had had an argument, and Gonzalez "tried to verbally restrain her from leaving the apartment."

Susana and Gonzalez's mother, who also lives in the building, were outside by the time the first two officers arrived, the claim says. When Gonzalez's mother returned from a short time outside, two more officers were stationed at the apartment door. The claim says none of the officers tried to solicit any information from Susana or Gonzalez's mother, including whether Gonzalez, who had isolated himself in a bathroom, had a weapon.
Gonzalez was unarmed and not impaired by alcohol or drugs. He was not behaving aggressively. Nor did he have a history of mental illness, the claim says.

"He posed no danger to himself, the (family members), the public or to any of the Defendant police officers on the scene," the claim says, also noting that both Gonzalez's wife and mother offered to speak to him in his first language, Spanish, to help defuse the situation, "which was continually being escalated by the arrival of additional police officers to the scene." But their offers were refused, according to the statement of claim.

Six additional Emergency Task Force officers, armed with riot shields, shot guns and a battering ram, arrived at the scene. One officer who spoke to Gonzalez's mother said he was "dangerous," even though there was no evidence to support this assertion, the claim says.

According to the claim, the police officers then "physically extricated" Gonzalez from his apartment bathroom, inflicting "grievous injuries" that included "multiple taserings and a brutal physical assault on him." Time-stamped surveillance footage from the building shows Gonzalez being taken out on a stretcher, his head rapidly moving from side to side.

Gonzalez was "barely conscious and largely unresponsive" to family members at the scene and had "severe facial, head and chest trauma and contusions along with two black eyes and electrocution injuries to his chest and groin," the claim says.

A spokesperson for the province's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which investigates incidents with the police involving serious injury or death, said the investigation into Gonzalez's death is "ongoing."

After the family of Rodrigo Gonzalez re-turned to the apartment, they took a video of the state of the bathroom they say Gonzales had isolated himself in when he was "extricated" by police who'd come in armed with riot shields, guns and a battering ram.
The Star previously reported that it took five days for SIU investigators to show up at the apartment, and nobody told the family to preserve the scene in the bathroom.

The family's lawyer, Kevin Wolf, said that while he and the family are "hopeful and optimistic" that the SIU's investigation will give them some answers, they do not believe it will necessarily "lead to full and frank disclosure of what happened that evening," because "subject officers" are not legally required to co-operate with SIU investigators.

("Subject officers" are the officers who appear to have caused the injury or death. "Witness officers" are officers who appear to have been involved in the incident but are not under investigation. They must submit to an interview and hand over a copy of their notes.)
In a civil proceeding, all officers will be compelled to be examined under oath, Wolf said.
"The (family) has suffered a permanent and deep loss of an integral member of their close-knit family," the claim says. "(They) will never fully recover from their loss."
~ With files from David Bruser
- Toronto Star
